title: Firefighters Use Fire to Save Giant Sequoias—And It Works!
summary: Did you know that some of the biggest trees on Earth—giant sequoias—can live over 3,000 years? But in 2020 and 2021, ferocious wildfires killed thousands of them. It was a shock, because sequoias have thick bark and are used to small fires. So what went wrong? Scientists discovered a surprising hero: more fire! But not the raging kind. For decades, park rangers have been doing prescribed burns—carefully set, low-intensity fires that clean up dead wood and bushes on the forest floor. A new study from UC Davis looked at sequoia groves hit by the Castle Fire and KNP Complex Fire. Using lasers from planes and satellite images, they checked about 26,400 trees. The result? Sequoias in areas that had prescribed burns in the last 10 years were nearly four times more likely to survive! Lead researcher Dan Dixon said, "Prescribed burns are effective at reducing giant sequoia mortality, even for today's extreme wildfires." The study estimated that prescribed burns saved about 1,900 trees. If all groves had been treated, another 3,900 might have lived. Think of it like cleaning your room: if you pick up clutter, a small accident won't turn into a disaster. By using fire wisely, we can protect these ancient giants from the very flames that threaten them.
why_it_matters: Just like cleaning your room prevents a small mess from becoming a disaster, prescribed burns help keep forests safe, which protects the world's biggest trees for future generations to enjoy.

background_read: Giant sequoias are the most massive trees on Earth, growing naturally only in California's Sierra Nevada. They have thick bark and rely on periodic low-intensity fires to release seeds and clear the forest floor.
Dan Dixon (a forest researcher at UC Davis, a university in California) and his team used airplane lasers and satellite photos to check the health of thousands of sequoias after two huge wildfires.
For many years, the U.S. National Park Service has used prescribed burns to reduce dangerous fuel buildup, mimicking the natural fire cycle that sequoias depend on.
Article_Structure: WHO: Researchers from UC Davis, led by Dan Dixon.
WHAT: Prescribed burns nearly quadrupled the survival chance of giant sequoias during extreme wildfires in 2020-2021.
WHERE: Sequoia groves in California that were burned by the Castle Fire and the KNP Complex Fire.
WHY: To find out if prescribed burns really protect these ancient trees from severe wildfires, and to show that more controlled fire could save thousands more.

perspectives.description: Using fire wisely can save these ancient trees, and it's a natural way to keep the forest healthy.
Some communities fear prescribed burns because they can produce smoke or might accidentally get out of control.
While prescribed burns help, they need to be done carefully and on a larger scale to protect all the groves from future mega-fires.
